body:
From the Buddha's teachings to different traditions

Buddhism began in northern India with the teachings of Gautama Buddha, who lived around the 6th–5th centuries BCE. His teachings attracted both people who renounced household life and people who continued to live as householders. Monks and nuns formed organised communities known as the Sangha, while lay followers supported them and practised Buddhist teachings in everyday life.

As Buddhism spread across different regions, its followers developed distinct ways of interpreting texts, organising religious life and pursuing liberation. These developments produced several Buddhist schools and traditions. Three broad traditions that remain especially important are Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana.

What the traditions share

All 3 traditions recognise Gautama Buddha as a central teacher. They accept the importance of ethical conduct, wisdom and the overcoming of suffering. They also retain the fundamental Buddhist understanding that attachment and ignorance contribute to suffering and that liberation requires spiritual practice.

The traditions differ chiefly in the spiritual ideals they emphasise, their collections of religious texts and the methods they use. These differences developed over centuries; they did not arise through a single division immediately after the Buddha's death.

The 3 major traditions

TraditionPrincipal emphasisRegions of prominence
TheravadaTeachings preserved in the Pali tradition; the ideal of the arahant or arhatSri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos
MahayanaThe bodhisattva path, compassion and the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beingsChina, Korea, Japan and Vietnam
VajrayanaThe Mahayana goal pursued through additional tantric practices, such as mantras and mandalasTibet, Bhutan, Nepal and Mongolia

These are broad regional associations, not exclusive geographical boundaries. Mahayana and Vajrayana practices also reached parts of Southeast Asia, while other forms of Buddhism continued to exist alongside them.

Understanding the historical sequence

The earliest Buddhist communities existed before the later classification into these 3 traditions. Theravada preserves a lineage connected with the ancient Buddhist schools, but it should not be treated as an exact synonym for every form of early Buddhism.

Mahayana developed within Indian Buddhism, with its distinctive ideas becoming increasingly visible around the beginning of the Common Era. Vajrayana subsequently developed within the wider Mahayana tradition, with tantric Buddhist practices becoming prominent in India during the early medieval centuries.

A distinction in terminology

Some Mahayana writings used the term Hinayana, meaning lesser vehicle, for other Buddhist paths. This is not a neutral or exact synonym for Theravada. Theravada is the established name of a living Buddhist tradition and should be used when that tradition is intended.

Prelims focus

  • Theravada means the teaching or tradition of the elders.
  • Mahayana means the great vehicle and particularly emphasises the bodhisattva ideal.
  • Vajrayana means the diamond or thunderbolt vehicle and is a tantric development within Mahayana.
  • Mahayana became increasingly visible around the beginning of the Common Era.
  • The 3 traditions share basic Buddhist teachings but differ in important ideals, texts and practices.
  • Trap: Theravada is not an exact synonym for all early Buddhism, and Vajrayana is not wholly separate from Mahayana.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapters 7 and 10, printed pp. 65–72 and 103–106; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, section 10.1, printed p. 103; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ethics in Indian Buddhism, section 2, 2024 revision, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Buddhist Traditions: Common Foundations and Historical Development

body:
Meaning and main spiritual ideal

Theravada is commonly translated as the teaching of the elders. The name expresses continuity with the teachings preserved and transmitted by respected early Buddhist teachers and monastic communities.

The tradition gives particular importance to ethical discipline, meditation and wisdom. A central spiritual ideal is the arahant, called an arhat in Sanskrit. An arahant is a person who has overcome the ignorance and craving that bind living beings to repeated birth and suffering and has attained liberation.

This ideal does not mean that Theravada rejects compassion or teaching others. Monks, nuns and lay followers may practise generosity, compassion and service to others. The emphasis on individual spiritual effort refers to the fact that liberation cannot be achieved merely by another person's actions.

The Pali Tipitaka

Theravada preserves a particularly important collection of Buddhist scriptures in Pali. The collection is called the Tipitaka, meaning 3 baskets. The equivalent Sanskrit term is Tripitaka.

  • Vinaya Pitaka: Rules and regulations governing the conduct and organisation of the monastic Sangha.
  • Sutta Pitaka: Discourses and teachings associated with the Buddha and his disciples.
  • Abhidhamma Pitaka: Systematic analysis of Buddhist teachings, especially matters of mind, experience and doctrine.

The 3 divisions are distinguished by subject matter. They should not be confused with 3 separate Buddhist schools.

Transmission to Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka became a major centre for the preservation and development of Theravada Buddhism. According to Sri Lankan Buddhist chronicles, the monk Mahinda travelled to Sri Lanka during the reign of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The mission is associated with the Sri Lankan king Devanampiya Tissa.

The same tradition associates Sanghamitta with bringing a branch of the sacred Bodhi tree to Sri Lanka and helping establish a community of Buddhist nuns. These accounts are important parts of Sri Lankan Buddhist historical tradition; their narrative details should not all be treated as independently established facts.

Spread across mainland Southeast Asia

Over time, Theravada became the dominant Buddhist tradition in Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos, as well as Sri Lanka. This expansion involved repeated contacts among monks, rulers, monasteries, merchants and pilgrimage centres. It was not the result of one mission reaching every country at the same time.

Sri Lanka played an important role in the transmission of Pali texts and monastic traditions. Local rulers and religious communities in mainland Southeast Asia subsequently supported Theravada monasteries and practices.

Distinguish the ideal from the language

The arahant is a spiritual ideal, while Pali is the language of Theravada's principal canonical collection. Neither term is the name of a separate Buddhist school.

Prelims focus

  • Theravada is especially associated with the arahant or arhat ideal.
  • The Tipitaka contains the Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitakas.
  • The Vinaya Pitaka concerns monastic discipline.
  • Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition associates Mahinda and Sanghamitta with the spread of Buddhism during Ashoka's period.
  • Theravada became prominent in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos.
  • Trap: The 3 Pitakas are divisions of scripture, not Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, section How Buddhist Texts Were Prepared and Preserved, printed p. 86; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 10, printed pp. 104–105; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ethics in Indian Buddhism, section 2, 2024 revision, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Theravada Buddhism: The Elders' Tradition, Texts and Spread

body:
The meaning of Mahayana

Mahayana means the great vehicle. It developed within Indian Buddhism, and its distinctive ideas became increasingly visible around the beginning of the Common Era. Mahayana continued to accept the importance of ethical conduct, meditation and wisdom while placing special emphasis on the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings.

The bodhisattva ideal

A bodhisattva is a being following the path towards Buddhahood. In Mahayana, the bodhisattva aspires to develop wisdom and compassion so that other beings can also be helped towards liberation.

Two qualities are particularly important:

  • Compassion: Concern for the suffering of other living beings and the commitment to help them.
  • Wisdom: Understanding reality correctly and overcoming ignorance, which is a cause of suffering.

The bodhisattva ideal does not mean that wisdom is abandoned in favour of compassion. Both are considered essential to the path. Nor is it accurate to define every bodhisattva simply as someone who has already attained complete Buddhahood.

Arhat and bodhisattva

The arhat is a liberated person who has overcome the causes of rebirth and suffering. The Mahayana bodhisattva follows a path directed towards Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The distinction concerns the ideal being particularly emphasised, not the presence or absence of compassion.

Buddhas, bodhisattvas and devotional practice

Mahayana traditions gave increasing importance to devotion to Buddhas and bodhisattvas. They also developed additional scriptures, often called Mahayana sutras. These texts were composed and transmitted in languages including Sanskrit and were later translated into other Asian languages.

Important bodhisattva figures include Avalokiteshvara, particularly associated with compassion, and Maitreya, recognised in Buddhist traditions as a future Buddha. Maitreya is not exclusive to Mahayana.

Early Buddhist art often represented events in the Buddha's life through symbols such as the Bodhi tree, an empty seat, footprints and the wheel of dhamma. From around the beginning of the Common Era, images of the Buddha in human form became increasingly important at centres such as Mathura in northern India and Gandhara in the north-west.

The increasing importance of Buddha and bodhisattva images is associated with developments in Mahayana Buddhism. However, the presence of a Buddha statue does not by itself prove that a monument belongs to Mahayana, because other Buddhist traditions also use images.

From India to East Asia

Mahayana spread from India through Central Asia to China, where Indian Buddhist scriptures were translated into Chinese. Buddhist learning subsequently spread further to Korea and Japan, while Vietnam developed Buddhist traditions through connections with China and other Asian networks.

Overland trade routes, particularly branches of the Silk Roads, connected merchants, Buddhist teachers and monasteries. These routes helped texts and teachings move between different regions. Local rulers and communities then supported the establishment of Buddhist institutions.

Prelims focus

  • Mahayana particularly emphasises the bodhisattva path towards Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings.
  • Avalokiteshvara is especially associated with compassion.
  • Maitreya is recognised as a future Buddha and is not exclusive to Mahayana.
  • Mathura and Gandhara were important early centres for images of the Buddha.
  • Mahayana became prominent in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
  • Trap: The existence of a Buddha image alone does not establish that a site belongs to Mahayana.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, section 10.1, printed p. 103; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 10, printed pp. 103–104; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 4, sections on Mathura and Gandhara, printed pp. 29–31; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ethics in Indian Buddhism, section 2, 2024 revision, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor, Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Mahayana Buddhism: The Bodhisattva Ideal and East Asian Transmission

body:
What Vajrayana means

Vajrayana means the diamond or thunderbolt vehicle. The Sanskrit word vajra refers to a diamond or thunderbolt and symbolises spiritual strength and the ability to overcome ignorance.

Vajrayana developed within the wider Mahayana Buddhist tradition. It shares the Mahayana aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. Its principal distinction lies in the additional methods used in spiritual practice, especially those associated with Buddhist tantra.

Tantric Buddhism

Tantric Buddhism uses prescribed ritual and meditation practices, often taught under the guidance of a qualified teacher, as part of the path to spiritual realisation.

Important Vajrayana practices

Several terms are especially useful for understanding the basic features of Vajrayana:

  • Mantra: A sacred formula or sequence of syllables recited as part of religious practice.
  • Mandala: A symbolic arrangement used in ritual or meditation to represent a sacred or enlightened order.
  • Mudra: A symbolic hand gesture used in ritual or religious representation.
  • Visualisation: A meditation practice involving carefully prescribed mental images.
  • Teacher-guided practice: Certain tantric practices are traditionally undertaken with instruction from an authorised spiritual teacher.

These methods do not replace all other Buddhist teachings. Vajrayana continues to emphasise ethical conduct, compassion and wisdom.

Development in India

Tantric Buddhist practices became increasingly important in India during the early medieval period, particularly from around the 6th–8th centuries CE onwards. Monasteries and Buddhist teachers in eastern India played important roles in developing and transmitting these traditions.

The Pala rulers, who governed parts of eastern India from approximately the 8th to the 12th century CE, supported major Buddhist institutions. They patronised Nalanda in Bihar and established or supported other centres, including Vikramashila, also in Bihar. Vikramashila became particularly associated with teachers learned in tantric Buddhist texts.

Nalanda was already an established centre of Buddhist learning before the Pala period; it was not founded by the Palas.

Spread to Tibet and neighbouring regions

Indian Buddhist teachers and texts were important in the transmission of Buddhism to Tibet. Tibetan Buddhist traditions particularly associate the consolidation of Buddhism in Tibet during the 8th century CE with King Trisong Detsen and teachers including Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava. Traditional accounts contain religious narratives as well as historical information, so every detail should not be treated as equally certain.

Vajrayana later became especially influential in Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal and Mongolia. Related esoteric Buddhist practices also developed in other parts of Asia, so Vajrayana is not confined exclusively to the Himalayan region.

Prelims focus

  • Vajrayana means the diamond or thunderbolt vehicle.
  • Vajrayana developed within Mahayana Buddhism.
  • Mantra means a sacred formula; mandala is a symbolic arrangement; mudra is a symbolic gesture.
  • The Pala rulers supported Buddhist learning in eastern India.
  • Nalanda and Vikramashila were important Buddhist institutions in Bihar.
  • Trap: The Palas patronised Nalanda but did not establish it.

[Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ethics in Indian Buddhism, section 2, 2024 revision, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 4, section on Ellora, printed pp. 41–42; Metropolitan Museum of Art, South Asia: North, 500–1000 A.D., Key Events, consulted 18 November 2026; Metropolitan Museum of Art, In the Footsteps of Buddhist Pilgrims: Sites in North India, section on Vikramashila, consulted 18 November 2026.]
